title: Singing it at dawn
hookLine: the full var with chhants takes about three hours at dawn

cards: It's still dark. The streets are empty except for a milk truck and a few people walking quickly, heads covered. Inside the gurdwara the lights are low and the floor is cool.
The Guru Granth Sahib has been opened for the day. A few dozen people sit cross-legged on white sheets, some in shawls, some with children asleep against them.
At the front, the ragis, the musicians, tune a harmonium and tap the tabla once. Then they begin a song that won't finish until the sky is fully light.

teach.h: SUNG EACH MORNING IN RAG ASA.
teach.b: In gurdwaras that keep the old morning order, the Asa di Var is sung every morning, in the hours around dawn, as part of the day's first kirtan. It has long been a fixed part of the morning program.
It's sung in Rag Asa, to the old tune we met on day five hundred thirty-seven, the ballad of a king. But what the sangat hears is longer than what you'd read in the Granth.

teach.h: GURU RAM DAS'S CHHANTS WOVEN IN.
teach.b: The ragis weave in the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru: twenty-four stanzas from his chhants in Rag Asa, one for each pauri.
So it goes something like this: a chhant of Guru Ram Das, sung slowly and lovingly; then the saloks; then Guru Nanak's pauri, gathering it all into a step; then the next chhant.
Sung in full, it can take around three hours. Some gurdwaras sing a shorter form, a few chhants or all of them, depending on the day and the ragis. Why dawn?

Gurbani calls the hours before sunrise amrit vela, the ambrosial time, and Japji speaks of meditating on the true Name and its greatness in those early hours. The mind hasn't filled up yet. The phone hasn't started.
And there's something about hearing wonder, awe, ego and sweetness sung while the sky goes from black to gray to gold. The var you've been studying word by word was never meant to stay on the page.
It was meant to be sung, slowly, with the sun coming up behind it.

how: In gurdwaras that keep the morning order, ragis sing Asa di Var around dawn, weaving Guru Ram Das's chhants between the saloks and pauris; the full form can take around three hours.

games.q: you're a ragi at a gurdwara before dawn. a pauri of the Asa di Var is coming up. what do you sing first?
o: a chhant of Guru Ram Das, then the saloks.
games.why: the pattern: a chhant of Guru Ram Das, then the saloks, then Guru Nanak's pauri, then the next chhant.

practice: Picture fifteen minutes before tomorrow's sunrise: where you'd sit, and what you'd hear, a recording of the Asa di Var or simply the quiet, while the window lightens.
Breathe slowly as you picture the color changing from black to gray to gold. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
